newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French unions disagree on strike prospects.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French unions disagree on strike prospects.

text.p: Two French union bosses disagreed on Tuesday over the prospects for a wave of labour unrest against government austerity plans intended to help France qualify for the planned single European currency.
But as 12.5 million pupils started the school year, the FEN -- France's biggest schoolteachers' union -- confirmed an earlier call for a national one-day strike between September 27 and October 3.
FEN leader Guy Le Neouannic urged other unions to pick a day for a joint protest and denounced government plans for 5,000 layoffs in education.

Polls show voters widely expect a new flare-up of labour unrest in France, perhaps matching a 21-day bout of public sector strikes in late 1995, that could challenge European Union plans for monetary union from 1999.

"I really don't see it happening," said Nicole Notat, head of the pro-Socialist CFDT, France's largest union group, when asked if she expected widespread unrest. But she predicted sporadic strikes in the autumn.

Louis Viannet of the pro-Communist CGT union, which spearheaded last year's strikes with the Force Ouvriere union, said the economic climate in France, especially over near-record unemployment, was "a catastrophe".

"There is every reason for expression of discontent and for increasing demands," he said. Those expecting a wave of unrest "are not wrong but that doesn't mean to say that it will happen automatically. There are no rules," he said.
He said voters were increasingly fed up in France since President Jacques Chirac's centre-right government was asking them to continue accepting the same policies of austerity.

"I'd be tempted to say that what's changed is that things are continuing. We're facing a president and a government who are broadly explaining to us: Things are going badly...we must continue the same policies with the same government."
Notat said the CGT was "very low-key" about the possibility of strikes. She also reiterated support for a single currency, saying it would help to create jobs.

France faces severe budget restrictions to qualify for the currency, but she said: "We must stop saying that it's difficult...People talk about the deficit reduction to forget that the single currency will bring positive things."
